sections.h2: What does phone ordering look like for a Latin American restaurant?
sections.body:
For a Latin American restaurant, phone ordering usually means the caller wants a quick pickup order, a delivery order, or a simple question about the menu. A good phone host should handle common items like tacos, rice bowls, pupusas, empanadas, roast chicken, sides, drinks, and add-ons without making the caller repeat themselves.

A practical phone flow looks like this:
1. The host answers and greets the caller.
2. The caller places the order item by item.
3. The host confirms size, modifiers, and notes.
4. The host asks for the caller’s name and phone.
5. The host quotes a ready time and repeats the order.
6. A clean ticket goes to the kitchen screen.

Example script line: "Thanks for calling. What can I get started for pickup or delivery today?" That one line matters because it gets the caller moving fast, which is what most phone orders need during lunch and dinner.

sections.h2: How do I keep the menu accurate for tacos, platters, and specials?
sections.body:
The easiest way to keep phone orders accurate is to make the live menu easy for the host to read. ROAL reads menu details from your website, Google Maps link, menu PDFs, menu photos, or anything you upload, then builds the phone host in about two minutes.

Use this checklist before you go live:
- Make sure item names match what your staff actually says on the phone.
- List sizes clearly, such as single, combo, half tray, or full tray.
- Mark sold-out items so the host does not offer them.
- Add common modifiers like extra sauce, no onions, or spice level.
- Add notes for popular specials and family platters.

Concrete example: if your menu has a $14.00 carne asada plate, a $3.00 side of rice, and a $2.00 extra salsa charge, the host should quote those exact prices. If you change the menu, update it in the dashboard so the next caller hears the right information.

sections.h2: How do bilingual calls help during a dinner rush?
sections.body:
Many Latin American restaurants get calls from both Spanish-speaking and English-speaking guests, sometimes in the same hour. A phone host that speaks the caller’s language can reduce confusion, especially for toppings, sides, pickup times, and address directions.

ROAL can speak the caller’s language and also hand off harder calls to staff with a summary. That is useful for:
- Catering requests
- Complaints
- Allergy-sensitive questions
- Manager requests

Example phone line: "Puedo ayudarle con su pedido. ¿Es para recoger o entrega?" You can also keep a simple bilingual FAQ ready for questions like parking, hours, and which menu items contain dairy, nuts, or shellfish. When the host cannot answer something, it lands in the inbox so the owner answers once and the host learns from it from then on.

sections.h2: What should I do about pickup, delivery, and payment?
sections.body:
For phone orders, pickup and delivery need different details. Pickup calls usually need the name, order, and ready time. Delivery calls need the address, phone number, and delivery notes, but the host should still keep the order clean and short.

ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it. That keeps the call simple and avoids forcing callers to read card details aloud.

Worked example you can swap for your own numbers:

sections.h2: How do I forward my restaurant number without changing it?
sections.body:
You do not have to abandon your existing number. With ROAL, the owner claims the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and the restaurant forwards its existing number to it. You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered, and turn forwarding off any time.

For many landlines and some carriers, *72 then the forwarding number forwards all calls, and *73 turns it off. On GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

Because codes vary by carrier and plan, confirm with your carrier and test with a real call. A simple test checklist:
- Call your main number from a cell phone.
- Confirm the host answers.
- Place a test order.
- Confirm the ticket appears on the kitchen screen.
- Turn forwarding off and confirm the old setup returns.

sections.h2: What should I watch on the dashboard each day?
sections.body:
The dashboard is where a busy owner can see what happened without digging through voicemail. ROAL includes a kitchen screen with live tickets marked new, preparing, and ready, plus call history with transcripts and recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus.

A simple daily routine:
1. Check the new tickets before opening.
2. Review any calls with questions the host could not answer.
3. Update hours if you have a holiday or an early close.
4. Add menu changes or sold-out items.
5. Review upsell suggestions for items customers often add.

If you run more than one spot, multi-location menus help keep each restaurant organized. A phone host for one location should not confuse the specials at another. That matters for groups with different lunch menus, different hours, or different phone lines.

sections.h2: Is a pay-per-order model a better fit than monthly phone plans?
sections.body:
For owners who only want to pay when the phone turns into a completed order, pay-per-order pricing can be easier to understand than a fixed monthly fee. Many AI phone answering products charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call.

ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free, and billing happens monthly.

Use this simple comparison with your own numbers:
| Example | Monthly cost formula |
|---|---|
| 30 completed orders | 30 × $0.90 = $27.00 |
| 80 completed orders | 80 × $0.90 = $72.00 |
| 150 completed orders | 150 × $0.90 = $135.00 |

If your phone gets a lot of questions but fewer completed orders, pay-per-order can be easier to match to actual business.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take Latin restaurant phone orders in Spanish and English?
faq.a: Yes. ROAL can speak the caller’s language and take orders, questions, and reservation requests in that language. That is especially helpful for Latin American restaurants where callers may switch between Spanish and English during the same call.

faq.q: Will the phone host offer items that are sold out?
faq.a: No. ROAL does not offer items marked sold out. If you update your menu or mark an item unavailable, the host will stop offering it on calls.

faq.q: How do I set up call forwarding for my restaurant number?
faq.a: Forwarding depends on your carrier or phone system. Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off, while some mobile carriers use different codes for busy or unanswered calls. Confirm the exact code with your carrier and test with a real call.
